solution:
Note that first factors of each term \(1, 3, 5, 7, \ldots\) are in A.P. with \(a = 1\), \(d = 2\).

\(t_{r} = a + (r-1)d = 1 + (r-1)2 = 2r - 1\).

Also the second factors \(5, 7, 9, 11, \ldots\) are also in A.P. with \(a = 5\), \(d = 2\).

\(t_{r} = 5 + (r-1)2 = 5 + 2r - 2 = 2r + 3\)

\(\therefore S_{n} = \displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n} (2r - 1)(2r + 3)\)

\(= \displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n} (4r^{2} + 4r - 3)\)

\(= 4 \displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n} r^{2} + 4 \sum_{r=1}^{n} r - \sum_{r=1}^{n} 3\)

\(= 4 \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} + 4 \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2} - 3n\)

\(= n\left[\dfrac{2(n+1)(2n+1)}{3}\right] + 2n(n+1) - 3n\)

\(= \dfrac{n}{3}\left[2(2n^{2} + n + 2n + 1) + 6(n+1) - 9\right]\)

\(= \dfrac{n}{3}\left[(4n^{2} + 6n + 2) + 6n - 3\right]\)

\(= \dfrac{n}{3}(4n^{2} + 12n - 1)\)

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2n^2 + 2n + 1\right)\). That is wrong at EVERY \(n\). The correct closed form is \(\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2n^2 + n + 1\right)\). Checked against the series summed term by term: at \(n = 1\) the true sum is \(2\) while the printed form gives \(\dfrac{5}{2}\), which is not even an integer; \(n = 2\) true \(11\) vs \(13\); \(n = 3\) true \(33\) vs \(\dfrac{75}{2}\); \(n = 4\) true \(74\) vs \(82\). The printed form passes 0 of 5 test values; the corrected form passes 5 of 5.]

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key is exactly the closed form of \(\sum r(2r+1)(2r+3)\) — the book used first factor \(r\) where the question prints \(2r - 1\). It AGREES with the true sum at \(n = 1\) (both \(15\)) and diverges from \(n = 2\) onward: true \(120\) vs \(85\), \(n = 3\) true \(435\) vs \(274\), \(n = 4\) true \(1128\) vs \(670\). A spot-check at the first term would certify the wrong answer, which is why several values must be tested. The printed form passes 1 of 5; the corrected form passes 5 of 5.]

stem: If \(\dfrac{1 \times 2 + 2 \times 3 + 3 \times 4 + 4 \times 5 + \ldots \text{ upto } n \text{ terms}}{1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + \ldots \text{ upto } n \text{ terms}} = \dfrac{100}{3}\), find \(n\).
If \(S_{1}\), \(S_{2}\) and \(S_{3}\) are the sums of first \(n\) natural numbers, their squares and their cubes respectively then show that \(9 S_{2}^{2} = S_{3}(1 + 8 S_{1})\).
